query: Eutectic high-entropy alloys contain dual-phase lamellar colonies with numerous internal boundaries, where microcracking can initiate and lead to catastrophic damage during room-temperature tensile deformation. Conventional processing commonly raises strength at the expense of ductility, while the wide range of previously proposed microstructural-design and processing strategies has not eliminated room-temperature brittleness and limited tensile ductility. Under these constraints, what single intervention could improve both strength and room-temperature tensile ductility? State one testable hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts outcomes relative to the unmodified lamellar-colony baseline, defines its boundary conditions, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Introducing a minor, targeted addition of a ductility‐promoting element (e.g., Nb) during alloy processing will drive interfacial segregation at the lamellar colony boundaries, thereby improving both tensile strength and room-temperature ductility compared to the unmodified state.
generation.material_initial_state: Eutectic high-entropy alloy with dual-phase lamellar colonies exhibiting conventional, chemically unmodified internal boundaries that are prone to microcracking under tensile deformation.
generation.intervention: Add a carefully controlled, minor concentration of a ductility‐enhancing element (such as Nb) during melting/solidification to promote segregation at the interphase boundaries without altering the overall eutectic lamellar structure.
generation.conditions: Process under conditions that maintain the dual-phase lamellar morphology while enabling targeted segregation (i.e., optimized melting, controlled cooling rates, and subsequent heat-treatment steps), with the elemental addition remaining below levels that might trigger unwanted secondary phases.
generation.structural_mediator: The chemically modified and strengthened interfacial regions between lamellar colonies that result from solute segregation.
generation.mechanism: The segregated element is expected to reduce localized stress concentrations and hinder crack initiation by improving the cohesion at phase boundaries. This modification simultaneously impedes dislocation motion, thereby increasing yield strength, while fostering more uniform plastic deformation to enhance ductility.
generation.predicted_outcome: The intervention should yield improved room-temperature tensile properties: both higher tensile strength and enhanced ductility relative to the untreated alloy, compared to the unmodified lamellar colony baseline.
generation.baseline: The unmodified eutectic high-entropy alloy with conventional, unsegregated interphase boundaries that exhibit microcrack initiation and limited tensile ductility.
generation.boundary: The beneficial effects are expected only within a narrow compositional window where the dopant promotes interfacial segregation without causing detrimental phase transformations or coarsening of the lamellar structure. Excess doping or incorrect processing parameters may negate the improvement or even worsen the brittleness.
generation.uncertainty: The optimal concentration of the dopant and exact processing parameters required to achieve the balance between enhanced strength and ductility remain to be determined experimentally.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of eutectic high-entropy alloy samples: one set with the minor addition of the ductility-promoting element (e.g., Nb) under controlled processing conditions designed to encourage interfacial segregation, and a control set without the intervention. Use transmission electron microscopy (TEM) and atom probe tomography (APT) to verify chemical segregation at the interphase boundaries. Perform room-temperature tensile tests on both sets to compare tensile strength and ductility, and analyze fracture surfaces to assess crack initiation.
measurements: Fractographic analysis (to determine crack initiation sites)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the samples with the targeted dopant addition do not show statistically significant improvement in both tensile strength and ductility compared to the control, or if interfacial segregation is not observed, then the hypothesis is falsified.
